description: Boiler tube thickness testing and ultrasonic tube inspection for US utility, HRSG, pulp mill and industrial boilers during outages. Request a UT quote.
h1: Boiler Tube Thickness Testing: Ultrasonic Tube Inspection for Boiler Outages in the United States
html:
Boiler tube thickness testing is a grid survey of tube wall with a calibrated ultrasonic gauge, done while the boiler is out of service. Atlantis NDT mobilizes ultrasonic technicians to utility, industrial, pulp mill and refinery outages across the United States, reads waterwall, superheater, reheater, economizer and HRSG tubes on the locations you mark, and returns a mapped record for your boiler inspector and engineers. Request a UT inspection quote with tube dimensions and outage dates.

Why boiler tubes are surveyed for wall thickness

A boiler tube leak ends a run, so owners survey tubes during outages to find thinning before it becomes a forced shutdown. The damage mechanisms differ by tube bank, and the survey follows them. On the fireside, waterwall tubes can thin from fireside corrosion, particularly in low-NOx firing arrangements, and from erosion around sootblowers and soot-cleaning lanes. In the convection pass, fly ash erodes tubes at gas-flow turns, baffles and the edges of tube banks. Economizer tubes can lose wall to ash erosion outside and, in some designs, to corrosion at the inside; in combined cycle heat recovery steam generators (HRSGs), flow-accelerated corrosion thins low-pressure evaporator and economizer tubes inside, and the thickness record shows it. Corrosion fatigue and cracking happen too, but a thickness gauge reads wall, not cracks, and a different examination applies.

That explains why the grid is wider than a handful of points. The thinning is rarely uniform, and the worst tube is often found only because the grid went past the expected area.

Codes, regulators and who decides

Boiler inspection in the United States is a mix of code and jurisdiction:

  • ASME Section I: power boilers, which sets the design wall and the code basis for minimum thickness.
  • NBIC Part 2: the National Board Inspection Code, which covers inspection and condition assessment of boilers in service and is used by state and insurance inspectors.
  • State boiler inspectors and insurers: each jurisdiction decides which boilers need an internal certificate inspection and by whom; see the National Board of Boiler and Pressure Vessel Inspectors for the system.
  • EPRI boiler tube failure guidance: industry guidance on damage mechanisms and where to look.
  • BLRBAC practices: the Black Liquor Recovery Boiler Advisory Committee guidelines used for recovery boilers at pulp mills.
  • ASTM E797 and ASME Section V Article 23: the thickness measurement practice behind the gauge technique.

The owner, its boiler inspector or its engineering group decides whether a tube is acceptable and what repair or replacement is needed. We give them the wall data and the map. Atlantis does not calculate remaining life, and we do not act as the commissioned inspector.

How the survey is laid out

A tube survey is a map before it is a measurement. The technician and your boiler engineer agree the zones to read: for example, waterwall panels by elevation and wall, sootblower lanes, burner corners, superheater and reheater pendant bottoms, economizer inlet rows, and the tubes near attachments, buckstays and welded lugs. Tubes are numbered from a reference tube at a fixed corner, and elevations are tied to a landmark such as a platform, burner level or buckstay. Readings are taken at a set pattern on each tube, and where a line of tubes is thin, the grid tightens around it.

Tubes are small in diameter and curved, so the probe, couplant and technique are chosen to suit. A small-footprint dual-element or delay-line probe sits properly on the tube crown; on the curve, readings are taken along the axis, and the technician notes if the probe rocks. The technique, probe, calibration block and surface condition are written into the procedure, which follows ASME Section V Article 23 and is approved by an ASNT Level III. If you need one written, see NDT technical procedure development.

Surface preparation, access and the outage

Ultrasonic readings on tubes depend on a clean fireside surface. Ash, slag and scale have to be removed at the reading point, normally by the site's cleaning contractor with water blasting, grit blasting or power-tool cleaning, followed by a light dressing so the probe seats. A tube with a heavy deposit reads thick and hides the real wall, which is why cleaning is usually the first schedule dependency in a boiler outage.

Access is the other. Waterwalls and convection passes are reached from scaffold, hanging platforms, climbers or rope access arranged and controlled by the site; the same applies to confined-space permits, lockout and tagout, and gas testing. During the outage the tubes are cold, so the high-temperature probes needed on live piping are not an issue here. We bring gauges, probes, blocks, couplant and recording sheets, and your site provides scaffold, lighting, cleaned surfaces and permits.

Recovery boilers at pulp mills need particular care. Floor and lower wall tubes in recovery boilers are inspected under BLRBAC practices, which are written by the industry for that hazard, and many have composite tubing in the lower furnace. Plain carbon-steel recovery boiler tubing can be gauged for wall; composite tubes need techniques that Atlantis does not offer.

Data and what the report contains

  • Unit name, boiler section, tube bank and panel, with a sketch or tube map and the tube numbering system
  • Tube outside diameter, nominal wall, material, and the minimum wall supplied by the owner or boiler engineer
  • Procedure number and revision, gauge, probe, couplant, calibration block and calibration checks
  • Technician name and level, with the written practice under which the qualification is held
  • Readings by tube and elevation, with the lowest reading per tube highlighted and tubes at or near minimum wall flagged
  • Surface condition, any areas not read, and comparison with the previous outage where you provide it

The data is formatted to load into your inspection records or boiler management system. The engineer uses the wall history to select tubes for replacement or shielding; our job is to make that history reliable.

Repeatability and reading discipline

Tube surveys are compared from outage to outage, sometimes by different crews, so repeatability matters more than any one reading. The technician marks each reading spot with paint or a scribe tick at the same clock position on the tube, usually the fireside crown where wastage is worst, and records the position in the notes. A reading on a tube at a different spot than last time can differ by several mils for reasons that have nothing to do with corrosion, because the wall is rarely uniform around the circumference.

The technician also watches for the signs that a reading is wrong: an unsteady display, a thickness that jumps between two values, or a reading far above nominal that suggests a deposit or a lamination rather than good wall. Suspect readings are repeated, cleaned and re-read, and where the doubt remains it is written into the report instead of being smoothed over. If your engineer wants the lowest of several readings per location, or the average, say so up front so the record shows the same convention at every tube.

What to send for a quote

  • Boiler type, unit number and operating pressure, with tube outside diameter, wall and material by bank
  • The tube map, previous survey data and minimum wall requirements
  • Zones to read and the pattern wanted, for example one reading per tube per row or a tighter grid at sootblowers
  • Outage dates, cleaning plan and who provides scaffold or rope access
  • Whether the unit is a utility boiler, industrial boiler, HRSG or pulp mill recovery boiler
  • Site address, badging, safety orientation and permit requirements

Where we work in the United States

Boiler outages follow generation and process industry footprints. These city pages have local detail on ultrasonic work:

  • Charlotte: Carolinas generating stations, from coal and gas steam units to combined cycle plants.
  • Knoxville: Tennessee Valley steam plants and industrial boilers.
  • Birmingham: Alabama utility units and the steel and pipe industry's own boilers.
  • Pittsburgh: Ohio and Beaver Valley power stations and mill boilers.
  • Mobile: Gulf Coast power, paper and chemical boilers along Mobile Bay.
  • Savannah: coastal Georgia pulp and paper mills and utility boilers.
  • Tampa: Florida gas-fired and combined cycle plants and phosphate-industry boilers.
  • Kansas City: Missouri and Kansas utility steam units and industrial boilers.

The sector pages go further: power generation, pulp and paper mills, chemical plants and refineries. The general ultrasonic inspection menu is at NDT inspection services, and the method overview is on the national ultrasonic testing page. For outage context see turnaround and shutdown inspection, and for the thickness standard, the guide to ASME Section V Article 5 thickness measurement.

What we do not do here

Radiographic testing is outside our scope in the United States, where industrial radiography needs a license under 10 CFR Part 34 or Agreement State rules. Oxide scale measurement and composite tube examination are specialist techniques that we do not offer on this page. We do not calculate remaining life, set inspection intervals or decide tube replacement; your boiler inspector and engineer do that from our data.

Training your own boiler inspection staff

If your plant wants in-house readings, our UT Level 1 training and UT Level 2 training teach gauge calibration, tube technique and recording, and the ultrasonic testing simulator offers repeatable practice. See also power generation NDT training. Under SNT-TC-1A the employer certifies its own people, so the course supports your written practice.

faq.q: How is boiler tube thickness tested?
faq.a: A technician cleans the tube surface at each reading location, calibrates an ultrasonic gauge on a block of the same alloy, and places a small probe on the tube with couplant. The gauge reads wall thickness, and readings are logged by tube number and elevation on a map.

faq.q: Is the boiler running when you test the tubes?
faq.a: No. Boiler tube surveys are done during an outage with the unit cold, cleaned and made safe by the site. Access, lockout, confined-space permits and scaffold are arranged by your plant before our technicians start.

faq.q: Can you tell me how much life is left in a tube?
faq.a: No. We provide wall thickness by tube and elevation, compared with the minimum wall and previous survey data you supply. Remaining life and replacement decisions are made by your boiler inspector or engineer.

faq.q: Do you measure oxide scale on superheater tubes?
faq.a: No. Oxide scale measurement is a specialist technique that we do not offer on this page. Ultrasonic wall thickness testing of the tube metal is what we provide.

faq.q: Can you inspect composite recovery boiler tubes?
faq.a: No. Composite tubes in pulp mill recovery boilers need specialist techniques that are not part of this service. Plain carbon-steel tubes can be gauged for wall, and the recovery boiler survey scope should be agreed with your BLRBAC program first.

faq.q: What cleaning is needed before testing?
faq.a: The fireside surface has to be free of ash, slag and loose scale at each reading point so the probe couples to metal. Water, grit or power-tool cleaning is normally arranged by the site, and a light dressing may be needed where the surface is pitted.

faq.q: What do you need to quote a tube thickness survey?
faq.a: Send the unit type, tube size, wall and material by bank, tube maps, previous survey data, minimum wall, zones to read, outage dates and who provides scaffold or rope access. Photos of typical tube condition help plan probes and surface preparation.

faq.q: Which codes apply to boiler tube inspection?
faq.a: ASME Section I covers design of power boilers, the National Board Inspection Code Part 2 covers in-service inspection, and state boiler laws set who inspects. The thickness technique follows ASTM E797 and ASME Section V Article 23.

faq.q: Can the same visit include weld or crack testing?
faq.a: Weld and surface crack checks are separate scopes, and we can add ultrasonic weld examination, magnetic particle testing or liquid penetrant testing to a visit where the method fits the material and the procedure. Tell us what is needed when you request a quote.
